title: The Career Cost of Being Too Humble
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: The author argues that letting the work speak for itself is a career mistake, because doing a good job and making sure people know about it are separate tasks. Drawing on a first decade of long hours and slow progression, she names the effort trap: talking about how hard you work instead of what you delivered. Her remedy has two parts. First, reframe contribution around impact and keep a running achievements log so the evidence is ready at review time. Second, reframe language by replacing hedged team phrasing with the first person while still crediting the team. She closes by redefining humility as fairness to others and to yourself.
points: The effort trap: describing hours worked instead of outcomes delivered gives a manager nothing to build a promotion case on.
An achievements log, kept all year, supplies concrete evidence when reviews, promotion asks or new opportunities come up.
Phrases like 'it was a team effort' hide your own role; saying 'I led' while crediting the team makes the contribution visible.
Humility is redefined as recognising your own contribution while giving credit to others, not as staying quiet.
quotes: Here’s what I’ve come to realise: in business, doing a good job and making sure people know you’ve done a good job are two very different things. And sometimes, if you leave the second part to chance, you can miss out.

The first tells people something about your ability, your skills and the value you bring. The second tells them you’re busy. And being busy, on its own, isn’t a particularly compelling argument for promotion.

I think we can be so worried about sounding boastful that we end up underselling ourselves. We downplay our contribution, give everyone else the credit or use language that makes our achievements sound much smaller than they actually are.
Teamwork is important and sharing credit is absolutely right. But there’s a difference between acknowledging the team and disappearing into it.
Don’t dismiss these things as just part of your job. They might be exactly the evidence someone needs to see that you’re ready for more.

It shouldn’t mean staying quiet about our successes or playing down our achievements. It should mean recognising our own contribution while giving credit to others, making sure everyone gets the recognition they deserve, including us.
